provenance.authorship: Original project scenario, AI-assisted draft. Practitioner review and calibration pending.

title: Security Analyst: Triage a Reported Phishing Message
prompt: You are a trainee security analyst at fictional Cedar Services. At 09:10 an employee reports a payroll email and says, "I opened the link and entered my work password, but I did not approve any sign-in prompt." The email is still available. Company procedure permits you to record a report and contact the on-call analyst; only that analyst may revoke sessions or isolate devices. Walk through your first ten minutes, explain what you would ask, and give the employee an update. This is a tabletop exercise.
blurb: Practice triage, evidence preservation, and a clear security handoff within a trainee’s authority.

rubric.label: Establish exposure
rubric.description: Separates a reported password disclosure from unverified compromise.

anchors.0: Dismisses the report because no approval prompt was accepted, or declares a confirmed breach without evidence.
anchors.2: Establishes what was entered and when and treats the credential disclosure as urgent.
anchors.4: Builds a short timeline, asks about downloads and sign-ins, and distinguishes confirmed exposure from questions for log review.

rubric.label: Act within authority
rubric.description: Preserves useful evidence and routes containment through the on-call analyst.

anchors.0: Opens the suspicious link, requests the password, or claims to revoke access without authority.
anchors.2: Preserves the email and promptly escalates the potential credential exposure.
anchors.4: Provides the on-call analyst a concise evidence package, requests authorized containment and its confirmation, and avoids destroying evidence.

rubric.label: Support and close the loop
rubric.description: Gives the employee clear, non-blaming next steps and a check-back.

anchors.0: Blames the employee or promises the account is safe without verification.
anchors.2: Thanks the employee, explains escalation, and asks them not to revisit the link.
anchors.4: States what is known, what the analyst will verify, and when the employee will hear back; checks whether interrupted work needs support.

reference.scenario: You are a trainee security analyst at fictional Cedar Services. At 09:10 an employee reports a payroll email and says, "I opened the link and entered my work password, but I did not approve any sign-in prompt." The email is still available. Company procedure permits you to record a report and contact the on-call analyst; only that analyst may revoke sessions or isolate devices. Walk through your first ten minutes, explain what you would ask, and give the employee an update. This is a tabletop exercise.

facts.value: The employee used their managed work laptop. They did not download a file and still have access to normal work services.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about device, downloads, or current impact

facts.value: The on-call analyst can respond in five minutes. The reporting tool can preserve the original email without opening its link; no sign-in logs are supplied yet.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks about escalation, evidence preservation, or logs

model_points: Treat entering a work password as a meaningful exposure even without an approved sign-in prompt. Ask for the time, affected account, downloads, and unexpected activity; do not ask the employee to repeat the password.

Preserve the original message using the reporting tool, record the report, and contact the authorized analyst immediately. Ask for review of sign-ins and authorized credential/session containment; do not claim these actions succeeded.
A useful handoff distinguishes the employee report from verified observations and names the pending checks. Keep communication calm so future reports remain likely.

probes.trigger: candidate says MFA means there is no risk
probes.question: What has already been exposed, even if the second factor was not approved?

probes.trigger: candidate lists many checks before escalation
probes.question: Which checks must happen before calling the analyst, and which can run afterward?

fair_alternatives: A direct call or the urgent incident channel is acceptable if it reaches the on-call analyst promptly and leaves a record.
Requesting a password reset through the approved support process is reasonable; direct execution is outside the trainee role.
red_flags: Dismisses the report because no approval prompt was accepted, or declares a confirmed breach without evidence.
Opens the suspicious link, requests the password, or claims to revoke access without authority.
Blames the employee or promises the account is safe without verification.
follow_ups: Write a four-line handoff separating reported exposure, preserved evidence, requested action, and next update.
reference.exemplar_answer: I would thank the employee and record that the password was entered at about 09:10; compromise is possible but not confirmed. I would preserve the email through our reporting tool, ask about downloads and unusual sign-ins, and call the on-call analyst now. I would request their account-containment and log-review process, explain to the employee not to reopen the link, and confirm our next update after the analyst responds.

interviewer_notes: Play the reporting employee initially, then the on-call partner when requested. Do not invent attacker activity or demand command syntax. Reward prompt escalation without requiring a named security framework. Use only supplied facts; say when something is unknown. Accept plain language and equivalent approaches. Assess the demonstrated decisions, not accent, confidence, credentials, or access to particular employers. This is a fictional exercise; do not imply real actions were performed.

learning_drills.title: Write the incident handoff
learning_drills.prompt: Write a four-line handoff separating reported exposure, preserved evidence, requested action, and next update. This is self-guided practice; no model assessment is performed.
checklist: Name the affected account without a secret
